topicName: Masked Arrays and Missing Data Handling
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Masked Arrays and Missing Data Handling in NumPy"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"In real-world data science and engineering tasks, missing or invalid data is a common occurrence. Standard NumPy arrays do not inherently handle missing values gracefully, often resulting in NaN pollution or requiring tedious boolean indexing. NumPy addresses this challenge via the numpy.ma module, which introduces masked arrays. A masked array is the combination of a standard numpy.ndarray and a boolean mask that flags elements as valid or invalid."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating Masked Arrays"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can create a masked array directly using the numpy.ma.array function, or by taking an existing array and applying a mask explicitly. Elements with a mask value of True are considered hidden or missing, while False indicates valid data."},{"order":6,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np
import numpy.ma as ma

# Create a basic array with an invalid value represented by -999
data = np.array([1.0, 2.0, -999.0, 4.0, 5.0])

# Mask the invalid value
masked_data = ma.masked_values(data, -999.0)
print(masked_data)"},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Explicit Masking and Inspection"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can also define a mask manually using boolean arrays. The masked array allows you to inspect the underlying data, the mask itself, and the valid data points using specific attributes."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"# Define data and a corresponding boolean mask
values = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
custom_mask = np.array([False, False, True, False, False])

# Create the masked array
m_arr = ma.array(values, mask=custom_mask)

print('Data:', m_arr.data)
print('Mask:', m_arr.mask)
print('Compressed (Valid only):', m_arr.compressed())"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Operations with Masked Arrays"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"When performing mathematical operations, NumPy automatically ignores masked values. Functions like mean, sum, and standard deviation will compute results based only on the unmasked elements."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"# Calculating statistics ignoring masked elements
readings = ma.array([12.5, 13.2, np.nan, 14.1, 15.0], mask=[False, False, True, False, False])

print('Mean:', readings.mean())
print('Sum:', readings.sum())"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices"},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always import numpy.ma as ma to keep namespace boundaries clear."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use ma.masked_invalid to automatically mask NaN and Inf values in floating-point arrays."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Remember that operations returning scalars will return masked scalar instances if the underlying data is invalid."}]
